sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes a well-preserved skull and partial skeleton of a relatively small dinosaur measuring about 5 meters in length.
Its skull features a unique lateral projection of the praemaxilla that curves downward at 165 degrees, alongside a large lower sleep window that is both taller and wider than the eye socket.
This animal holds the distinction of being the first known hadrosaurid skull discovered in Appalachia.
The large lower sleep window, being wider and taller than the eye socket, represents a striking anatomical feature.
The fossil MSC 7949 was discovered in 2007 within the Upper Santonian layer of the Mooreville Chalk Formation in Alabama.
The species Eotrachodon orientalis was officially named and described in 2016 by Albert Prieto-Márquez, Gregory M. Erickson, and Jun A. Ebersole.
The skull possesses a derived nasal bone structure that may be a precursor to the form seen in Saurolophinae.
The discovery of Eotrachodon suggests that the typical nasal structure of saurolophines developed early, shortly after their divergence from lambeosaurines.
The genus Eotrachodon was established by Prieto-Márquez, Erickson, and Ebersole in 2016 and is classified within the dinosaur family Hadrosauridae.
In phylogenetic analysis, Eotrachodon is placed as a basal member of Hadrosauridae, positioned above Hadrosaurus and as the sister taxon to Saurolophidae.
Eotrachodon lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 83 million years ago in the Santonian stage, in what is now North America.
The fossil record for this genus spans from 85.7 to 83.6 million years ago during the Santonian stage.
There is a taxonomic debate regarding the classification of this lineage, with some researchers using the term Saurolophidae while others refer to it as Euhadrosauria.
